title: Volumes & Arc Length
summary: Solids of revolution have volume by disks/washers $\int\pi(R^2-r^2)\,dx$ or cylindrical shells $\int2\pi(\text{radius})(\text{height})\,dx$. Arc length integrates $\sqrt{1+(f')^2}$, and surface area adds a $2\pi r$ factor.

solid of revolution.plain: A shape made by spinning a region about a line.
solid of revolution.in_class: Volume via disks, washers, or shells.

disk method.plain: Slices perpendicular to the axis, no hole.

washer method.plain: Slices with a hole (region away from the axis).

cylindrical shells.plain: Nested thin cylinders parallel to the axis.

axis of revolution.plain: The line the region spins around.
axis of revolution.in_class: Sets the radius in each formula.

arc length.plain: The true length of a curve.

surface area.plain: Area of a surface of revolution.

representative slice.plain: The generic thin piece you sum.
representative slice.in_class: Disk, washer, or shell — model it, then integrate.

concept_sections.heading: Disks and washers
concept_sections.explanation: Spin a region about an axis and slice perpendicular to it. A solid slice is a disk ($\pi R^2$); a slice with a gap is a washer ($\pi(R^2-r^2)$). Integrate along the axis.

concept_sections.heading: Cylindrical shells
concept_sections.explanation: Slice parallel to the axis into thin cylindrical shells of radius (distance to axis) and height (curve). Unrolled, each is a rectangle: $V=\int 2\pi(\text{radius})(\text{height})\,dx$.
math_steps: Identify each shell's radius and height.

concept_sections.heading: Choosing disks vs shells
concept_sections.explanation: Match the slice to the geometry: if slices perpendicular to the axis are simple, use disks/washers; if parallel slices are simpler (or the axis is offset), use shells.
math_steps: See which slicing avoids solving for the other variable.

concept_sections.heading: Arc length
concept_sections.explanation: Sum tiny hypotenuses $\sqrt{dx^2+dy^2}=\sqrt{1+(f')^2}\,dx$ along the curve: $L=\int_a^b\sqrt{1+(f'(x))^2}\,dx$.

concept_sections.heading: Surface area of revolution
concept_sections.explanation: Spinning a curve sweeps a surface; each band has area $2\pi r$ times the arc-length element: $S=\int 2\pi r\sqrt{1+(f')^2}\,dx$, with $r$ the distance to the axis.
math_steps: Multiply the arc-length element by $2\pi r$.

real_world_examples.title: Volume of a wine barrel
real_world_examples.scenario: A curved profile spun into a solid.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Disk/washer integration of the profile gives the barrel's volume.

real_world_examples.title: Length of a suspension cable
real_world_examples.scenario: A hanging cable follows a curve.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Arc-length integration measures the true cable length for material estimates.

real_world_examples.title: Surface area of a dome
real_world_examples.scenario: A curve revolved into a dome shape.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The surface-area integral gives how much material covers the dome.
